lesson.title: Branches: The Paths Current Travels
lesson.summary: A branch is a single path in a circuit through which one current flows, forming the basic building block used to describe how charge moves through more complex networks.
lesson.body:
You already know that current is the rate at which charge flows past a point, but in any circuit more complicated than a single loop, that charge has to travel along specific paths to get from one place to another. A branch is simply one such path: a stretch of the circuit, usually containing a single element like a wire, resistor, or source, that connects two points and carries one well-defined current. Think of a branch as a segment of "circuit road" ,  charge enters at one end and exits at the other, and along the way there is no side street for it to peel off onto.

That last point is the key mechanism to understand, not just memorize. Because a branch has no intermediate point where the path splits or merges with another path, the amount of charge entering it in any stretch of time must equal the amount leaving it in that same stretch. Charge doesn't pile up or vanish inside a plain wire or a single resistor. So if you measure the current at one end of a branch, you will measure the exact same current at the other end, no matter how long or short the branch is, or what element sits inside it. This is why we can talk about "the current in a branch" as a single number, rather than needing to specify where along the branch you measured it.

Branches become especially useful once a circuit has more than one path available to the current. Picture a battery connected to a single wire that runs to a junction point, and from that junction two separate wires continue on to do different jobs before eventually reconnecting. The stretch from the battery to the junction is one branch, and each of the two wires leaving the junction is its own separate branch. Suppose the battery branch carries a current of 5 amps. When that current reaches the junction, it has to divide between the two outgoing branches ,  say 2 amps goes down one branch and 3 amps down the other. Each of those branches now carries its own steady current (2 amps in one, 3 amps in the other), and neither value changes as you follow that branch along its length, for the same charge-continuity reason as before. The two branch currents add back up to the original 5 amps, simply because every bit of charge that arrived at the junction has to leave it somehow ,  but the deeper reasoning for exactly how currents split and recombine at junctions is something you'll formalize soon; for now, just notice that a branch is the unit that keeps a single current value intact.

It's worth being precise about what does and doesn't count as "inside" one branch. A stretch of circuit containing several elements connected one after another, with no junctions in between, still counts as a single branch, because current has nowhere else to go along that stretch ,  it's forced to be the same everywhere in it. The moment you hit a point where three or more wires meet, that point marks the end of one branch and the start of others. Getting comfortable with spotting where branches begin and end is what will let you later break down complicated-looking circuits into a handful of simple, single-current pieces, which is exactly the skill you'll need for analyzing how those pieces interact.
